overview: French Guiana’s history comes into view through ancient fields, cooking equipment, family records and living traditions of craft and celebration.

periods.title: An early settlement on the lower Maroni
periods.summary: The Chemin Saint-Louis excavators identified occupation around 50 to 220 CE. This is one archaeological window within a much longer Indigenous history, not the beginning of settlement throughout the region.

periods.title: Coastal farming landscapes
periods.summary: Late precolonial communities shaped raised fields and occupied nearby higher ground. Dating connects several studied sites with the early second millennium; this broad phase does not assign all fields one date.

periods.title: Colonial settlements and plantation society
periods.summary: French settlements developed from around 1620. This broad colonial phase includes competing European claims and enslaved labour, alongside continuing Indigenous communities; it was not one unchanged administration.

periods.title: First abolition
periods.summary: The revolutionary abolition of slavery took effect in Guyane in 1794. This freedom was later overturned.

periods.title: Slavery reinstated
periods.summary: Reinstatement proceeded in stages from November 1802 through June 1804. It was not simply one decree applied everywhere on the same day.

periods.title: Portuguese occupation
periods.summary: Portuguese occupation lasted from 1809 to 1817, interrupting French colonial government.

periods.title: French colonial government resumes
periods.summary: Portuguese occupation ended in 1817. Slavery continued under restored French colonial administration until abolition in 1848.

periods.title: Emancipation and new records
periods.summary: Abolition in 1848 ended legal slavery. Registers of newly freed people preserve names and other personal details from this transition.

periods.title: A colony with penal establishments
periods.summary: Penitentiaries and labour camps developed from 1852. They became a major part of colonial Guyane, alongside the communities whose lives extended far beyond prison institutions.

periods.title: Departmental status and later changes
periods.summary: The law of March 19, 1946 established departmental status. This broad period includes subsequent regional institutions and reforms, rather than an immediate, uniform change in everyone’s circumstances.

periods.title: Combined territorial institutions
periods.summary: The territorial collectivity installed on January 1, 2016 combined departmental and regional responsibilities within France.

sections.title: Discoveries: pots, fields and traces of food

items.text: At Chemin Saint-Louis on the lower Maroni, archaeologists found pottery vessels fitted inside one another in a pit. The site included occupation around 50 to 220 CE. Some pottery carried a red coating and geometric incisions. Its unfamiliar forms raised questions about local development and outside influence; a striking pot alone does not settle where its maker came from.

At K-VIII near Kourou, ancient farmers built raised plots and long ridges in a seasonally flooded landscape. Their arrangement varied with the ground: researchers interpret some ridges as helping drainage and others as retaining water. Farming involved shaping the land as well as planting seeds. These fields belong to a wider late precolonial landscape, with dates varying by site.

Tiny plant traces help reconstruct food history. Researchers identified maize remains in raised-field soils, squash at Piliwa, and maize and manioc starch on griddle fragments from Sable Blanc. The last traces connect particular cooking surfaces with crops. A fragment too small to hold your lunch can still preserve clues about someone else’s.

sections.title: Skilled work and care at Loyola

items.text: At Loyola in Rémire-Montjoly, Jesuits operated a plantation from 1668 to 1764 using enslaved labour. Excavation of its forge yielded hoes, hooks, hinges and locks. Unfinished hoe blades show stages in shaping an agricultural tool. These finds reveal skilled work, although they cannot identify which individual made or used each object.

Excavation beside Loyola’s kitchen recovered thousands of pottery fragments. A masonry cooking structure called a potager and a bread oven also survived. Here, potager means a place for heating cooking pots, rather than a vegetable garden. These remains reveal a particular plantation kitchen, not the meals or equipment available to everyone who lived and worked there.

Loyola’s hospital stood against its kitchen. Archaeologist Nathalie Cazelles suggests that the arrangement may reflect a belief that warmth hastened recovery. The building layout is evidence; that explanation is an interpretation. Neither proves that the treatment worked, nor that enslaved patients experienced the institution as benevolent.

Registers made for newly freed people in 1848 to 1853 preserve names, ages, occupations and places. The Manioc research project makes these details searchable and connects the work with questions about individuals and families. Official paperwork can help recover a person’s story, while remaining a partial account written within the institutions of its time.

At Boniville and Loka, Aluku heritage houses include timber walls, steep gabled roofs and often a carved front gable called a koppo. The preservation project links buildings with family and community history. It also brings apprentices together with local experts and carpenters. Saving a house can mean passing on the knowledge needed to make its next repair.

At Antecume Pata, the Yépé association’s workshops have taught basketry, weaving and pottery since 2015. The park reports that around thirty children participated in 2017, with Wayana and Apalaï craftspeople guiding their work. Young adults also learned to make objects for sale. Learning here involves watching skilled hands, practising and gradually making something of your own.

On April 9, 1968, a Véronique sounding rocket became the first rocket launched from the Guiana Space Centre. The flight tested the new launch site’s operating systems and recovery at sea of its radio-equipped payload. Space work began with practical trials on the ground and in the atmosphere, before the centre’s satellite-launching era.

The 2017 carnival inventory describes Touloulou costumes that conceal identity with dresses, masks, head coverings and gloves. Some participants even change their usual perfume. Women in these disguises invite partners to dance at the bal paré-masqué. Recognizing a friend can require more detective work than simply spotting their favourite shoes.

Carnival also has a social life around the table. The 2017 inventory describes sharing filled galettes des Rois with family, colleagues, schoolmates and associations during the season. A small token is hidden in the pastry, and finding it helps decide who provides refreshments next time. That slice of cake may come with a future hosting assignment.

ending.text: The 1946 departmental law changed French Guiana’s administrative status; combined territorial institutions followed in 2016 within France. These changes did not end its communities. Craft teaching, family memory and celebrations continue to connect generations.
